bottomLine.label: Bottom line
bottomLine.lead: Stable credit with thin headroom: leverage is falling, but the 2028 notes need refinancing before the engine programme pays back.
bottomLine.rest: Halden converts a strong order book into cash more slowly than its margin suggests. We see no liquidity pressure for eighteen months. The view rests on aftermarket pricing holding and on the unsecured notes being refinanced by mid 2027.

sides.heading: For and against
sides.note: Three points on each side, as the modules weighed them

items.text: Net leverage fell from 4.9x a year earlier as EBITDA grew faster than debt.
Aftermarket share of gross profit; it held through the last two downturns in build rates.
No maturity above USD 50m before the 2028 notes, and the facility is undrawn.
Unsecured notes fall due in 2028 with no refinancing agreed and coupons likely to reset higher.
Interest cover leaves little room if floating rates stay where they are.
Revenue from one engine programme whose ramp has slipped twice.

findings.body: Leverage fell by 0.3x in the year. Almost all of it came from EBITDA growth; net debt rose after the Corvane Fasteners purchase.
Working capital absorbed USD 71m as inventory was built for the engine ramp. Free cash flow covered interest but little else.

findings.lead: Pricing power sits in the aftermarket
findings.body: Sole-source parts carry most of the profit. Original-equipment contracts are fixed-price and thinner than peers.

findings.lead: The 2028 notes are the first real test
findings.body: The term loan and secured notes run to 2030 and 2031. The unsecured notes come first and rank behind both.
Only a springing first-lien covenant applies, and only when the facility is more than 40% drawn. It is far from tested.

changeView.title: Two triggers, either is enough
changeView.text: Net leverage back above 5.0x at a year end, or no refinancing of the 2028 unsecured notes agreed by 30 June 2027. Either would move the view to negative.

bottomLine.label: Bottom line
bottomLine.lead: A sole-source aftermarket franchise carries a thinner, more cyclical original-equipment business.
bottomLine.rest: The aftermarket earns most of the profit and is hard to displace. The risk is concentration: one engine programme and three customers decide whether growth arrives on time.

findings.body: Parts and repair bring 44% of revenue and about three fifths of gross profit. Most parts are sole-source and certified to the airframe.

findings.lead: Original equipment is thin and fixed-price
findings.body: New-build contracts run five to seven years at fixed prices. Margin here is below every listed peer.
Three customers bring 58% of revenue and one engine programme 34%. Its ramp has slipped twice.

findings.lead: Purchases have added breadth, not scale
findings.body: Four small purchases since 2023 added product lines. None changed the competitive position.

contrary.title: Two airlines have begun certifying alternative parts
contrary.text: If approved, alternatives would cover about a tenth of aftermarket revenue. Management says none has passed certification; the module could not confirm this from the files provided.

changeView.title: Loss of sole-source status on a top-ten part
changeView.text: One certified alternative on a top-ten part, or a third slip in the engine programme’s ramp, would move this module’s view from stable to weakening.

records.title: Questions this module set out to answer

items.question: How durable is aftermarket pricing?
items.answer: Durable for the parts where Halden is the only certified source, which carry about three fifths of gross profit. Price rises of 4 to 6% a year have held since 2021.

items.question: How exposed is revenue to one programme?
What share of contracts can pass through cost inflation?
How much of the order book is firm?
items.answer: About four fifths of the order book is under firm contracts, and the rest is covered by framework agreements that set prices but not volumes. The engine programme is firm to 2029, the repair contracts run on annual renewals, and the module could not tell how much of the framework volume has been called off since 2024, which the files do not show.

records.title: How a programme delay reaches the credit

gapsLink.label: See this module’s gaps in Evidence

items.text: Customer names and contract terms come from management presentations, not from contracts. Where a presentation and the annual report disagree the module used the annual report.

The share of revenue under cost pass-through clauses is not established for this run. The annual report describes pass-through as applying to “most long-term agreements” without a figure, the lender presentation gives a figure for the aftermarket only, and the two segment definitions differ, so the module did not combine them. The finding on input cost inflation therefore rests on the margin record of the last four years and not on contract terms, and it would not hold if the contract mix has changed since the 2024 renewals, which the files do not show.

bottomLine.label: Bottom line
bottomLine.lead: Demand is growing and certified supply stays tight.
bottomLine.rest: Traffic is above its earlier peak, and certification keeps new suppliers out of the aftermarket for years.

findings.body: A new supplier needs about three years to certify one part.
